title: The Seven Conditions Recited at Rajgir

title_i18n.en: The Seven Conditions Recited at Rajgir

subtitle: How a question of war became a charter of endurance
figure: Vassakara, Ananda and the Vajji Confederation
era: Vajji-Magadha rivalry, c. 5th century BCE; text fixed by c. 350-320 BCE
moral: Institutions endure when their habits endure.

sources.citation: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta, section on Vassakara's visit
sources.note: Primary Pali account of the seven conditions for Vajji welfare.

sources.citation: Anguttara Nikaya 7.21-22, Vajji Sutta; Chinese Dirghagama parallel
sources.note: Independent textual parallels for the same political teaching.

sources.citation: Oskar von Hinuber, A Handbook of Pali Literature (1996); Romila Thapar, Early India (2002); J.P. Sharma, Republics in Ancient India (1968)
sources.note: Modern dating and interpretation of republican institutions.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of Rajagriha's hill and fort, with Vassakara in foreground looking toward distant Vajji lands

dialogue.text: In Rajagriha, as Magadha eyed the Vajji confederation, a minister’s question drew from the Buddha seven habits said to keep a republic from decline.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of Rajagriha’s city nestled among hills, early morning light

dialogue.text: In the fifth century before the Common Era, the eastern plains were a patchwork of powers: monarchies like Magadha, and gana-sanghas like the Vajji confederation.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a simple royal office, Vassakara seated with palm-leaf documents, maps on a low table

dialogue.text: Magadha’s king Ajatashatru sought to expand his realm. To his minister Vassakara he entrusted a hard question: could the Vajji gana-sangha be broken?

panels.shot: slow push-in on Vassakara’s thoughtful face, interior dimly lit

dialogue.speaker: Vassakara of Magadha
dialogue.text: If they stand together, my king’s chariots may not be enough.

panels.shot: wide shot of the Bamboo Grove monastery near Rajagriha, monks moving between trees, Vassakara at the edge

dialogue.text: The Pali sources remember a different move. Vassakara went not to a war council, but to the Buddha’s retreat near Rajagriha, seeking insight before steel.

panels.shot: medium shot of Vassakara seated respectfully before an unseen elder figure, focus on his posture and humility

dialogue.speaker: Vassakara of Magadha
dialogue.text: Can Magadha, lord, defeat the Vajji, if it should attack?

panels.shot: close-up on Vassakara listening, face tilted, as if hearing a measured reply

dialogue.text: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta does not give a direct yes or no. It preserves instead a teaching: first to a disciple, Ananda, and through him, to all who would hear.

panels.shot: wide shot on a hillside near Rajagriha, the Buddha’s figure implied in silhouette, Ananda beside, Vassakara at a respectful distance

dialogue.text: The tradition places the scene on the eve of the Buddha’s last journey. Around him, disciples gathered; beyond, Magadha and Vajji watched one another in uneasy balance.

panels.shot: medium shot focusing on Ananda’s attentive face opposite the implied Buddha, Vassakara blurred in background

dialogue.text: To Ananda, the Teacher is said to have spoken first of the Vajjis, not as enemies, but as a people held together by certain habits.

panels.shot: slow push-in on the elder’s hand raised in gentle emphasis, Ananda’s hands folded, Vassakara listening

dialogue.text: The texts list seven conditions for the Vajjis’ welfare: that they assemble often, meet in concord, honour their ancient customs, and obey their elders.

panels.shot: montage-like wide shot of a Vajji assembly hall in Vaishali, elders seated in a circle, younger men standing respectfully around

dialogue.text: The gana-sangha of Vajji was no open democracy. It was an assembly of clans and elders, yet its strength lay in gathering frequently and in ending debate without rancour.

panels.shot: wide shot of the same hall, now showing elders greeting one another, a sense of continuity and ritual

dialogue.text: The Pali canon remembers them as faithful to their old decisions, and as a body that respected its senior members, preserving continuity even as generations turned.

panels.shot: montage wide showing Vajji women walking safely in the streets of Vaishali, shrines and trees in the background

dialogue.text: The seven conditions include this too: that women and young girls be protected, that shrines be cared for, and that ascetics be honoured and welcomed.

panels.shot: medium shot of an ascetic being respectfully offered alms at a Vajji village gate, elders watching approvingly

dialogue.text: Anguttara Nikaya and Chinese parallels echo this picture. Care for religious sites and wandering renunciants was counted among the habits that kept the Vajjis united.

panels.shot: medium shot back in the grove, Ananda reciting the seven conditions aloud to Vassakara, the elder seated silently

dialogue.text: According to the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha bids Ananda recite these seven points in Vassakara’s hearing, as if to answer the minister without advising war.

panels.shot: close-up on Vassakara’s face, thoughtful and slightly troubled, as he processes the implications

dialogue.speaker: Vassakara of Magadha
dialogue.text: A people bound so, my king should not meet by chariot alone.

panels.shot: wide shot of Vassakara taking his leave from the grove, bowing slightly, monks in the background

dialogue.text: The sutta tells that Vassakara left, understanding that as long as the Vajjis kept these habits, their decline would be hard to bring about.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye wide of the plains between Magadha and Vajji, with faint markers for rivers and cities, a sense of looming conflict

dialogue.text: Later traditions speak of a long war between Magadha and Vajji, even of sixteen hard years, but historians treat such numbers with caution, hearing in them the echo of memory rather than a record.

panels.shot: medium shot of a later monk copying palm-leaf manuscripts in a monastery, suggesting the fixing of the text

dialogue.text: By around the fourth century BCE, the discourse had taken shape in the canon, preserving not a verbatim court transcript, but a Buddhist memory of what held a republic together.

panels.shot: wide shot juxtaposing a modern legislative hall faintly superimposed with the ancient Vajji assembly, time-spanning composition

dialogue.text: Modern scholars see in the Vajjis an aristocratic gana-sangha, not a full democracy, yet the seven conditions still speak of how institutions endure when their habits endure.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Vassakara’s earlier silhouette against the hills, fading into the text-copying monk, suggesting continuity of questions

dialogue.text: A Magadhan minister seeking a way to break a rival left behind, through a monk’s memory, a different legacy: a warning that it is the daily habits of a people that decide whether their house stands or falls.
